scenes.narration: Money, luck and timing all played their parts in the life of Franklin D. Roosevelt — in that order. Franklin Delano Roosevelt (January 30, 1882 – April 12, 1945), also known as FDR, was the 32nd president of the United States, serving from 1933 until his death in 1945. He is the longest-serving US president and the only one to have served more than two terms.

The turning point in the life of Franklin D. Roosevelt looked like a failure at the time. His first two terms centered on combating the Great Depression, while his third and fourth focused on US involvement in World War II. A member of the Democratic Party, Roosevelt served in the New York State Senate from 1911 to 1913 and as the 44th governor of New York from 1929 to 1932.

Every biography of Franklin D. Roosevelt has to pass through the years that were quietly lost. Born into the prominent Delano and Roosevelt families, Roosevelt graduated from Harvard University. He was elected to the New York State Senate in 1910, before becoming the assistant secretary of the Navy under President Woodrow Wilson in 1913.

The education of Franklin D. Roosevelt happened mostly outside any school. Cox on the Democratic ticket in the 1920 presidential election, which Cox lost to Republican nominee Warren G. However, partly through the encouragement of his wife Eleanor, he was elected governor of New York in 1928.

What Franklin D. Roosevelt wanted at the start and what Franklin D. Roosevelt got are not the same thing, and that gap is the story. Roosevelt defeated President Herbert Hoover in a landslide victory in the 1932 presidential election. During his first 100 days as president, Roosevelt initiated the program to implement the New Deal, built the New Deal coalition, and realigned American politics into the Fifth Party System.

The defining trait of Franklin D. Roosevelt was not talent — it was the refusal to stop. He created programs to provide relief to the unemployed and farmers while seeking economic recovery with the National Recovery Administration and other programs. Major surviving programs and legislation implemented under Roosevelt include the Securities and Exchange Commission, the National Labor Relations Act, and Social Security.

Those who met Franklin D. Roosevelt at the peak describe someone still running on the early hunger. In 1940, he was reelected, as there were no presidential term limits until 1951. Following the Japanese attack on Pearl Harbor on December 7, 1941, Roosevelt obtained a declaration of war on Japan, and subsequently on Nazi Germany and Fascist Italy.

The private years of Franklin D. Roosevelt explain the public decades better than any speech. Roosevelt supervised the mobilization of the American economy to support the war effort and implemented a Europe first strategy. He also initiated the development of the first atomic bomb and worked with the other Allied leaders to lay the groundwork for the United Nations.

The family Franklin D. Roosevelt came from matters more than the legends admit. Since then, some of his actions have been criticized, such as his ordering of the internment of Japanese Americans. Nonetheless, historical rankings consistently place him among the three greatest American presidents.

The first real success of Franklin D. Roosevelt arrived later than anyone expected, and changed everything. Franklin Delano Roosevelt was born on January 30, 1882, in Hyde Park, New York, to James Roosevelt I and his second wife, Sara Ann Delano. James, "a wealthy, landed gentleman who dabbled in but usually devoted no great effort to business", was a prominent Bourbon Democrat.

The last chapter of Franklin D. Roosevelt was written long after the fame. Franklin had a half-brother, James Roosevelt "Rosy" Roosevelt, from his father's previous marriage. According to Alan Brinkley, the family lived "in a manner reminiscent of the English aristocracy, and Franklin grew up, therefore, in a remarkably cosseted environment, insulated from the normal experiences of most American boys".

The whole life of Franklin D. Roosevelt reads like a single decision repeated. Frequent trips to Europe and Canada helped Roosevelt become conversant in German and French. Aside from a stint in public school in Germany at age nine, Roosevelt was homeschooled by tutors until age 14.

Between the birth and the legend of Franklin D. Roosevelt lie the years that actually decide it. Its headmaster, Endicott Peabody, preached the duties of Christians and urged his students to enter public service. Peabody remained a strong influence throughout Roosevelt's life, officiating at his wedding and presiding over the church service which preceded his inauguration as president.

The reputation of Franklin D. Roosevelt was built in the middle, not at the edges. He was a member of the Alpha Delta Phi fraternity "Fly Club", though he regretted not being admitted to the Porcellian Club. Roosevelt was relatively undistinguished as a student or athlete, but he became editor-in-chief of The Harvard Crimson newspaper.

Somebody like Franklin D. Roosevelt should not have made it — that is exactly why the story survives. Theodore's vigorous leadership style and reforming zeal made him Franklin's role model. Franklin graduated from Harvard in three years in 1903 with an A.B. in history.

The life of Franklin D. Roosevelt begins far from where the story usually starts. Roosevelt entered Columbia Law School in 1904, but dropped out in 1907 after passing the bar. While at college, Roosevelt met and proposed to the heiress Alice Ruggles Sohier, who declined.

Franklin D. Roosevelt was not born famous — the early years shaped everything that followed. Franklin then began courting his childhood acquaintance and fifth cousin once removed, Eleanor Roosevelt, a niece of Theodore Roosevelt. Despite "initial resistance" from his mother, Franklin and Eleanor Roosevelt were married on March 17, 1905.

To understand where Franklin D. Roosevelt ended up, start with where Franklin D. Roosevelt began. Theodore, who was then President, gave away the bride since Eleanor's father Elliott was deceased. Franklin's mother, Sara Roosevelt, also provided a townhouse for the newlyweds in New York City, and had a house built for herself alongside that townhouse.

The road from the beginning to the peak of Franklin D. Roosevelt ran through years nobody filmed. Eleanor never felt at home in the houses at Hyde Park or New York City. However, she loved the family's vacation home on Campobello Island, also a gift from Sara.

Each stage of the life of Franklin D. Roosevelt made the next stage possible. Burns indicates that young Franklin Roosevelt was self-assured and at ease in the upper class. On the other hand, Eleanor was shy and insecure, and initially focused on her husband's career.

The people who knew Franklin D. Roosevelt young describe someone already restless. As his father had done, Franklin left childcare to his wife, and Eleanor assigned the task to caregivers. Elliott was born in 1910, another son named Franklin followed in 1914, and the youngest, John, was born in 1916.

What Franklin D. Roosevelt built in the middle years is what the name still stands for. He commenced an affair with Eleanor's social secretary, Lucy Mercer, soon after she was hired in 1914. Franklin contemplated divorcing Eleanor, but Sara objected, and Mercer would not marry a divorced man with five children.

By the time Franklin D. Roosevelt reached the defining moment, the preparation was decades old. Franklin promised never to see Mercer again, but their marriage shifted to become a political partnership. Eleanor soon established a separate home in Hyde Park at Val-Kill and devoted herself to social and political causes independent of her husband.

The rise of Franklin D. Roosevelt was not an accident — in retrospect the pattern is plain. Roosevelt's son Elliott claimed that his father also had an affair with his private secretary, Missy LeHand. In 1908, Roosevelt took an unsalaried position with the prestigious law firm of Carter Ledyard & Milburn, later moving into the firm's admiralty law division.

Setbacks came early for Franklin D. Roosevelt, and the response to them is the real story. Roosevelt cared little for the practice of law and told friends he planned to enter politics. Despite his admiration for cousin Theodore, Franklin accepted an invitation to run for the Democratic Party in the 1910 elections for the New York State Assembly.

The legacy of Franklin D. Roosevelt outlived the circumstances that produced it. He was a compelling candidate due to his name recognition and his family's ability to contribute to party fundraising, but his campaign ended after the Democratic incumbent, Lewis Stuyvesant Chanler, chose to seek re-election. Rather than putting his political hopes on hold, Roosevelt ran for a seat in the New York State Senate.

Few lives travel as far as that of Franklin D. Roosevelt, and the distance is the point. The senate district, located in Dutchess, Columbia, and Putnam Counties, was strongly Republican. Roosevelt feared that opposition from Theodore could end his campaign, but Theodore encouraged his candidacy despite their party differences.

The childhood of Franklin D. Roosevelt contains the adult in small print. Acting as his own campaign manager, Roosevelt traveled throughout the senate district via automobile at a time when few could afford a car. In the Democratic landslide in the 1910 United States elections, Roosevelt won a surprising victory.

Money, luck and timing all played their parts in the life of Franklin D. Roosevelt — in that order. Despite short legislative sessions, Roosevelt treated his new position as a full-time career. Taking his seat on January 1, 1911, Roosevelt soon became the leader of the "Insurgents" in opposition to the Tammany Hall machine that dominated the state Democratic Party.

The turning point in the life of Franklin D. Roosevelt looked like a failure at the time. In the 1911 US Senate election, Roosevelt and nineteen other Democrats caused a prolonged deadlock by opposing the Tammany-backed candidate. News articles and cartoons depicted "the second coming of a Roosevelt" sending "cold shivers down the spine" of Tammany Hall.

The education of Franklin D. Roosevelt happened mostly outside any school. After the election, he chaired the Agriculture Committee; his work on farm and labor bills was a precursor to his later New Deal policies. Roosevelt's support of Wilson led to his desired appointment in March 1913 as Assistant Secretary of the Navy, the second-ranking official in the Navy Department after Secretary Josephus Daniels, who tended towards pacifism.

What Franklin D. Roosevelt wanted at the start and what Franklin D. Roosevelt got are not the same thing, and that gap is the story. Roosevelt was enthusiastic (sometimes to the point of insubordination) and "an impassioned promoter of the Navy" who "viewed himself as a vital voice for national defense". Daniels and Roosevelt instituted a merit-based promotion system and extended civilian control over the autonomous departments of the Navy.
